<!-- Definition and medical uses -->
'''Omega-3-acid ethyl esters''' are a mixture of [[ethyl eicosapentaenoate]] and ethyl docosahexaenoate, which are ethyl esters of the [[omega−3 fatty acid]]s [[eicosapentaenoic acid]] (EPA) and [[docosahexaenoic acid]] (DHA) found in [[fish oil]].<ref name=AHFS2019/> Together with dietary changes, they are used to treat [[hypertriglyceridemia|high blood triglycerides]] which may reduce the risk of [[pancreatitis]].<ref name=AHFS2019/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Karalis DG | title = A Review of Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Hypertriglyceridemia: A Focus on High Dose Omega-3 Fatty Acids | journal = Advances in Therapy | volume = 34 | issue = 2 | pages = 300–323 | date = February 2017 | pmid = 27981496 | pmc = 5331085 | doi = 10.1007/s12325-016-0462-y }}</ref> They are generally less preferred than [[statin]]s, and use is not recommended by [[NHS Scotland]] as the evidence does not support a decreased risk of [[heart disease]].<ref name=AHFS2019/><ref name=BNF76/><ref name=EMA2019/> Omega-3-acid ethyl esters are taken by mouth.<ref name=AHFS2019>{{cite web |title=Omega-3-acid Ethyl Esters Monograph for Professionals |url=https://www.drugs.com/monograph/omega-3-acid-ethyl-esters.html |website=Drugs.com |publisher=American Society of Health-System Pharmacists |access-date=13 April 2019 }}</ref>

<!-- Side effects and mechanisms -->
Common side effects include burping, nausea, and an upset abdomen.<ref name=AHFS2019/><ref name=BNF76/> Serious side effects may include liver problems and [[anaphylaxis]].<ref name=AHFS2019/> While use in [[pregnancy]] has not been well studied, some omega−3 fatty acids appear beneficial.<ref name=Preg2019>{{cite web |title=Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids Use During Pregnancy |url=https://www.drugs.com/pregnancy/omega-3-polyunsaturated-fatty-acids.html |website=Drugs.com |access-date=13 April 2019 }}</ref> How it works is not entirely clear.<ref name=AHFS2019/>

Experts found a dose-dependent increase in the risk for atrial fibrillation in patients with cardiovascular diseases or cardiovascular risk factors who were being treated with omega-3-acid ethyl esters compared with those treated with placebo. The observed risk was at its highest at a dose of 4 g/d.[https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/997348?ecd=socpd_fb_rem-traf_mscp_2024Apr11-ABIMGMSCOUS1H_BAA-Id997348_md_dormant_englang-global-top8-int&form=fpf]

<!-- History and culture -->
Omega-3-acid ethyl ester medicines were approved for medical use in the European Union in 2000 and in the United States in 2004.<ref name=AHFS2019/><ref name=EMA2019>{{cite web |title=Omega-3 fatty acid medicines |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/referrals/omega-3-fatty-acid-medicines |website=European Medicines Agency |date=17 September 2018 |access-date=13 April 2019 }}</ref><ref name="FDA approval">{{cite web | title=Drug Approval Package: Omacor (Omega-3-Acid Ethyl Esters) NDA #021654 | website=U.S. [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA) | date=24 December 1999 | url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2004/21-654_Omacor.cfm | access-date=15 May 2020 | archive-date=2 February 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202225833/https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2004/21-654_Omacor.cfm | url-status=dead }}</ref> Beyond the branded prescription formulation, it is also available as a [[generic medication]] and [[over the counter]].<ref name=AHFS2019/><ref name=BNF76>{{cite book|title=British national formulary: BNF 76|date=2018|publisher=Pharmaceutical Press|isbn=978-0-85711-338-2|pages=206–207|edition=76}}</ref> In 2023, it was the 222nd most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 1{{nbsp}}million prescriptions.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Top 300 of 2023 | url=https://clincalc.com/DrugStats/Top300Drugs.aspx | website=ClinCalc | access-date=12 August 2025 | archive-date=12 August 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250812130026/https://clincalc.com/DrugStats/Top300Drugs.aspx | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title = Omega-3-acid Ethyl Esters Drug Usage Statistics, United States, 2014 - 2023 | website = ClinCalc | url = https://clincalc.com/DrugStats/Drugs/Omega3AcidEthylEsters | access-date = 20 August 2025 }}</ref>

==Medical use==
Omega-3-acid ethyl esters are used in addition to changes in diet to reduce [[triglyceride]] levels in adults with severe (≥ 500 mg/dL) [[hypertriglyceridemia]].<ref name="Lovaza FDA label" /> In the European Union and other major markets outside the US, omega-3-acid ethyl esters are indicated for hypertriglyceridemia by itself, or in combination with a [[statin]] for people with mixed [[dyslipidemia]].<ref name=emc>{{cite web | work = Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) |  publisher = Electronic Medicines Compendium (EMC) | title = Omacor | date=11 December 2019 | url=https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/medicine/10312 | access-date=15 May 2020}}</ref><ref name=EMA2019 />

Intake of large doses (2.0 to 4.0 g/day) of long-chain omega−3 fatty acids as prescription drugs or dietary supplements are generally required to achieve significant (> 15%) lowering of triglycerides, and at those doses, the effects can be significant (from 20% to 35% and even up to 45% in individuals with levels greater than 500 mg/dL).  It appears that both eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) lower triglycerides, but DHA appears to raise [[LDL cholesterol]]  more than EPA, while DHA raises [[High-density lipoprotein|HDL cholesterol]] while EPA does not.<ref name="NLApt2-2015">{{cite journal | collaboration =  NLA Expert Panel | vauthors = Jacobson TA, Maki KC, Orringer CE, Jones PH, Kris-Etherton P, Sikand G, La Forge R, Daniels SR, Wilson DP, Morris PB, Wild RA, Grundy SM, Daviglus M, Ferdinand KC, Vijayaraghavan K, Deedwania PC, Aberg JA, Liao KP, McKenney JM, Ross JL, Braun LT, Ito MK, Bays HE, Brown WV, Underberg JA | display-authors = 6 | title = National Lipid Association Recommendations for Patient-Centered Management of Dyslipidemia: Part 2 | journal = Journal of Clinical Lipidology | volume = 9 | issue = 6 Suppl | pages = S1–122.e1 | date = 2015 | pmid = 26699442 | doi = 10.1016/j.jacl.2015.09.002 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Other fish oil-based drugs===
Other omega−3 fish oil-based prescription drugs on the market have similar uses and mechanisms of action.<ref name=2014rev/>

* [[Ethyl eicosapentaenoic acid]] (Vascepa). EPA-only ethyl esters.<ref>{{cite web | work = CenterWatch | url = http://www.centerwatch.com/drug-information/fda-approved-drugs/drug/1215/vascepa-icosapent-ethyl | title = Vascepa (icosapent ethyl) | access-date = 31 March 2016 | archive-date = 5 August 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190805014955/https://www.centerwatch.com/drug-information/fda-approved-drugs/drug/1215/vascepa-icosapent-ethyl }}</ref>
* [[Omega-3-carboxylic acids]] (Epanova). This product contains free fatty acids, not ethyl esters.<ref>{{cite web|title=Epanova (omega-3-carboxylic acids)|url=http://www.centerwatch.com/drug-information/fda-approved-drugs/drug/1324/epanova-omega-3-carboxylic-acids|work = CenterWatch|access-date=15 December 2014|archive-date=25 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141225155451/http://www.centerwatch.com/drug-information/fda-approved-drugs/drug/1324/epanova-omega-3-carboxylic-acids}}</ref> It is currently withdrawn from the market by the manufacturer (AstraZeneca) and is thus unavailable to patients.<ref>{{cite book |author=Food and Drug Administration, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research |date=2021 |title=Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations |edition=41 |url=https://fda.gov/media/71474/download |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190504230543/https://www.fda.gov/media/71474/download |archive-date=4 May 2019 |publisher=Food and Drug Administration |page=830}}</ref> AstraZeneca voluntarily discontinued Phase III clinical trials for futility.<ref name="reuters20">{{cite news |title=AstraZeneca to discontinue Epanova trial, expects $100 million writedown |url=https://in.reuters.com/article/us-astrazeneca-study/astrazeneca-to-discontinue-epanova-trial-expects-100-million-writedown-idINKBN1ZC0JQ |access-date=15 January 2020 |work=Reuters |date=13 January 2020 |archive-date=14 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200114232904/https://in.reuters.com/article/us-astrazeneca-study/astrazeneca-to-discontinue-epanova-trial-expects-100-million-writedown-idINKBN1ZC0JQ }}</ref>

===Dietary supplements===
There are many fish oil dietary supplements on the market.<ref name=2015CompareRev/> There appears to be little difference in effect between dietary supplement and prescription forms of omega−3 fatty acids as to ability to lower triglycerides, but the ethyl ester products work less well when taken on an empty stomach or with a low-fat meal.<ref name=NLApt2-2015/>  The ingredients of dietary supplements are not as carefully controlled as prescription products and have not been tested in clinical trials as such drugs have.<ref name=emedDrugs>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sweeney ME | url = http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/126568-treatment#d8 | title = Hypertriglyceridemia Pharmacologic Therapy | journal = Medscape Drugs & Diseases | veditors = Khardori R | date = 14 April 2015 }}</ref> Prescription omega−3 products are more concentrated, requiring fewer softgels for the same daily dose.<ref name="2015CompareRev">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ito MK | title = A Comparative Overview of Prescription Omega-3 Fatty Acid Products | journal = Pharmacy and Therapeutics | volume = 40 | issue = 12 | pages = 826–57 | date = December 2015 | pmid = 26681905 | pmc = 4671468 }}</ref> Dietary fish oil is often esterified and then molecularly distilled to attain higher purity and/or concentration. Typical 'concentrated' fish oil supplements have doubled contents of EPA/DHA (ca. 50-65%). There are also products on the market with even higher concentrations of EPA/DHA (ca. 65-85%), labelled with 'triple', 'ultra', or similar wording. Some producers also provide backward conversion of FAE to triglyceride form in assumption of its higher bioavailability, these products usually have 'rTG' in their names.

In people with CKD who require hemodialysis, there is a risk that [[vascular blockage]] due to [[Coagulation|clotting]], may prevent dialysis therapy from being possible. [[Omega−3 fatty acid]]s contribute to the production of [[eicosanoid]] molecules that reduce clotting. However, a Cochrane review in 2018 did not find clear evidence that omega−3 supplementation has any impact on the prevention of vascular blockage in people with CKD.<ref name="Tam_2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Tam KW, Wu MY, Siddiqui FJ, Chan ES, Zhu Y, Jafar TH | title = Omega-3 fatty acids for dialysis vascular access outcomes in patients with chronic kidney disease | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2018 | issue = 11 | article-number = CD011353 | date = November 2018 | pmid = 30480758 | pmc = 6517057 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD011353.pub2 | collaboration = Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Group }}</ref> There was also moderate certainty that supplementation did not prevent hospitalization or death within a 12-month period.<ref name="Tam_2018" />

==Side effects==
Special caution should be taken with people who have [[Fish Allergy|fish and shellfish allergies]].<ref name="Lovaza FDA label" /> In addition, as with other omega−3 fatty acids, taking omega-3-acid ethyl esters puts people who are on [[anticoagulants]] at risk for prolonged [[bleeding time]].<ref name="Lovaza FDA label" /><ref name=NLApt2-2015/>

Side effects include [[Dyspepsia|stomach ache]], burping, and a bad taste; some people on very high doses (8g/day) in clinical trials had [[atrial fibrillation]].<ref name="Lovaza FDA label" />

Omega-3-acid ethyl esters have not been tested in pregnant women and are rated [[Pregnancy category#United States|pregnancy category C]]; it is excreted in breast milk and the effects on infants are not known.<ref name="Lovaza FDA label" />

==Pharmacokinetics==
After ingestion, omega-3-acid ethyl esters are metabolized mostly in the liver like other dietary fatty acids.<ref name=emc/>

Ethyl esters and triglycerides of omega−3 fatty acids show similar rates of absorption while monoglycerides and free fatty acids are absorbed significantly better.<ref name="2021kinetcs2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chevalier L, Vachon A, Plourde M | title = Pharmacokinetics of Supplemental Omega-3 Fatty Acids Esterified in Monoglycerides, Ethyl Esters, or Triglycerides in Adults in a Randomized Crossover Trial | journal = J Nutr | volume = 151 | issue = 5 | pages = 1111–1118 | date = May 2021 | doi = 10.1093/jn/nxaa458 | pmid = 33564872 | pmc = 8112767 }}</ref> Absorption rates depend on the mode of consumption and fat content of the following/accompanying meal. This may explain discrepancies in results of different studies.<ref name="2021kinetcs2"/>

==Mechanism of action==
Omega-3-acid ethyl esters, like other omega−3 fatty acid-based drugs, appears to reduce production of triglycerides in the liver and to enhance clearance of triglycerides from circulating [[very low-density lipoprotein]] (VLDL) particles. The way it does that is not clear, but potential mechanisms include increased [[Beta oxidation|breakdown of fatty acids]]; inhibition of [[diglyceride acyltransferase]], which is involved in biosynthesis of triglycerides in the liver; and increased activity of [[lipoprotein lipase]] in blood.<ref name=emc/><ref name=2014rev>{{cite journal | vauthors = Weintraub HS | title = Overview of prescription omega-3 fatty acid products for hypertriglyceridemia | journal = Postgraduate Medicine | volume = 126 | issue = 7 | pages = 7–18 | date = November 2014 | pmid = 25387209 | doi = 10.3810/pgm.2014.11.2828 | s2cid = 12524547 }}</ref> The synthesis of triglycerides is reduced in the liver because EPA and DHA are poor substrates for the enzymes responsible for triglyceride synthesis.

==Physical and chemical properties==
The active ingredient is concentrated omega-3-acid ethyl esters that are made from [[fish oil|fish body oils]] that are purified and [[esterification|esterified]].<ref name=adis/> For the Lovaza product, each 1000 mg softgel capsule contains 840 mg omega−3 fatty acids: [[eicosapentaenoic acid]] ethyl ester (460 mg) and [[docosahexaenoic acid]] ethyl ester (380 mg).<ref name=emc/>

==History==
Pronova BioPharma ASA had its roots in Norway's [[Cod liver oil|codfish liver oil]] industry. The company was founded in 1991 as a spinout from the JC Martens company, which was founded in 1838 in Bergen, Norway.<ref>{{cite web | work = Epax | url = http://www.epax.com/pages/history | title = 170 Year History | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160123032313/http://www.epax.com/pages/history | archive-date = 23 January 2016 | access-date = 31 March 2016 }}</ref> Pronova developed the concentrated omega-3-acid ethyl esters formulation that is the [[active pharmaceutical ingredient]] of Lovaza.<ref name=adis>{{cite web | work = Adis Insight | publisher =  Springer Nature Switzerland AG | url = http://adis.springer.com/drugs/800002488 | title = Omega-3 ethylester concentrate }}</ref>

Pronova won approvals to market the drug, called Omacor in Europe (and initially in the US), in several European countries in 2001 after conducting a three-and-a-half-year trial in 11,000 subjects;<ref>{{cite web | work = Pharma Times | date = 22 March 2001 | url = http://www.pharmatimes.com/Article/01-03-22/Pronova_wins_Omacor_approval.aspx | title = Pronova wins Omacor approval | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160414033701/http://www.pharmatimes.com/Article/01-03-22/Pronova_wins_Omacor_approval.aspx | archive-date = 14 April 2016 }}</ref> The company partnered with other companies like [[Laboratoires Pierre Fabre|Pierre Fabre]] in France.<ref>{{cite web | work = ICIS Chemical Business | date = 26 March 2001 | url = http://www.icis.com/resources/news/2001/03/26/135355/omacor-approved/ | title = Omacor approved }}</ref> In 2004, Pronova licensed the US and Puerto Rican rights to Reliant Therapeutics, whose business model was in-licensing of cardiovascular drugs.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Ernst A | work = Law360 | date = 27 November 2007 | url = http://www.law360.com/articles/40998/german-court-invalidates-omega-3-drug-patent | title = German Court Invalidates Omega-3 Drug Patent }}</ref> In that same year, Reliant and Pronova won FDA approval for the drug,<ref name=PBM2005>{{cite web | author1 = VHA Pharmacy Benefits Management Strategic Healthcare Group | author2 = Medical Advisory Panel | date = October 2005 | url = http://www.pbm.va.gov/clinicalguidance/drugmonographs/Omega3acidethylestersLovazaformerlyOmacor.pdf | work = National PBM Drug Monograph | title = Omega-3-acid ethyl esters (Lovaza, formerly Omacor) | access-date = 1 April 2016 | archive-date = 22 December 2016 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20161222180834/http://www.pbm.va.gov/clinicalguidance/drugmonographs/Omega3acidethylestersLovazaformerlyOmacor.pdf }}</ref> and it was launched in the US and Europe in 2005. Global sales in 2005 were $144M, and by 2008, they were $778M.<ref>{{cite web | work = Pharmaceutical Technology | url = http://www.pharmaceutical-technology.com/projects/pronova-biopharma/ | title = Pronova Biopharma Pharmaceutical Production Facility, Denmark | access-date = 31 March 2016 }}</ref>  In 2007 [[GlaxoSmithKline]] acquired Reliant for $1.65 billion in cash.<ref>{{cite web | work = Genetic Engineering News | date = 21 November 2007 | url = http://www.genengnews.com/gen-news-highlights/gsk-to-acquire-reliant-pharmaceuticals-for-1-65b/27018604/ | title = GSK to Acquire Reliant Pharmaceuticals for $1.65B }}</ref>

In 2009, generic companies [[Teva Pharmaceuticals]] and [[Par Pharmaceutical]] made clear their intentions to file [[Abbreviated New Drug Application]]s ("ANDAs") to bring generics to market, and in April 2009, Pronova sued them from infringing the key US patents covering Lovaza, US 5,656,667 (due to expire in April 2017), US 5,502,077 (exp March 2013). Subsequently, in May 2012, a district court ruled in Pronova's favor, saying that the patents were valid.<ref>{{US patent|5656667}}</ref><ref>{{US patent|5502077}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | publisher = Pronova BioPharma | date = 29 May 2012 | url = http://www.evaluategroup.com/Universal/View.aspx?type=Story&id=298783 | work = Press Release | title = US District Court rules in Pronova BioPharma's favour on Lovaza(TM) patents | access-date = 1 April 2016 | archive-date = 28 August 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210828195313/https://www.evaluate.com/ }}</ref> The generic companies appealed, and in September 2013, the Federal Circuit reversed, saying that because more than one year before Pronova's predecessor company applied for a patent, it had sent samples of the fish oil used in Lovaza to a researcher for testing. This event thus constituted "public use" that invalidated the patent in question.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Davis R | work = Law360 | date = 12 September 2013 | title = Fed. Circ. Nixes Pronova's Patent Win Against Teva, Par | url = http://www.law360.com/articles/472235/fed-circ-nixes-pronova-s-patent-win-against-teva-par }}</ref><ref>{{cite court |litigants= Pronova Biopharma Norge AS v. Teva Pharmaceuticals, Inc, USA and Par Pharmaceutical, Inc. and Par Pharmaceutical Companies, Inc. |vol=  |reporter=  |opinion=  |pinpoint=  |court= United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit 2012-1498, -1499 |date= 12 September 2013 |quote=  |url= http://c.ymcdn.com/sites/www.bpla.org/resource/resmgr/Biotech/Pronova%20Biopharma%20Norge%20v%20Teva%20Pharma%20FC%2012Sept2013.pdf |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160424205445/http://c.ymcdn.com/sites/www.bpla.org/resource/resmgr/Biotech/Pronova%20Biopharma%20Norge%20v%20Teva%20Pharma%20FC%2012Sept2013.pdf |url-status= bot: unknown }}</ref> [[Generic drug|Generic]] versions of Lovaza were introduced in America in April 2014.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Staton T | work = FiercePharmaMarketing | date = 9 April 2014 | url = http://www.fiercepharmamarketing.com/story/teva-puts-gsk-and-amarin-notice-generic-lovaza-launch/2014-04-09 | title = Teva puts GSK and Amarin on notice with generic Lovaza launch }}</ref>

Pronova has continued to manufacture the ingredients in Lovaza, and in 2012, [[BASF]] announced it would acquire Pronova for $844 million.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = McBride R | work = FierceBiotech | date = 21 November 2012 | url = http://www.fiercebiotech.com/story/basf-snap-fish-oil-drugmaker-pronova-biopharma-844m-buyout/2012-11-21 | title = BASF to snap up fish oil drugmaker Pronova BioPharma in $844M buyout }}</ref> The deal closed in 2013.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Palmer E | work = FierceManufacturing | date = 22 January 2013 | url = http://www.fiercepharmamanufacturing.com/story/basf-lands-pronova-making-it-top-omega-3-maker/2013-01-22 | title = BASF lands Pronova making it a top omega-3 maker }}</ref>

== Society and culture ==
=== Brand names ===
* Lovaza (US)/Omacor (Europe).<ref>{{cite web | url = http://pharmacyservices.utah.edu/alerts/251.html | work = University of Utah Pharmacy Services | date = 15 August 2007 | title = Omega-3-acid Ethyl Esters Brand Name Changed from Omacor to Lovaza | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303225225/http://pharmacyservices.utah.edu/alerts/251.html | archive-date = 3 March 2016 }}</ref> It was approved in the United States in 2004.<ref name=Ito2015>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ito MK | title = A Comparative Overview of Prescription Omega-3 Fatty Acid Products | journal = P & T | volume = 40 | issue = 12 | pages = 826–857 | date = December 2015 | pmid = 26681905 | pmc = 4671468 }}</ref>
* Omtryg is another brand of omega-3-acid ethyl esters developed by Trygg Pharma, Inc. and was approved by the FDA in 2014.<ref>{{cite web | title=Drug Approval Package: Brand Omtryg capsules NDA 204977 | website=U.S. [[Food and Drug Administration]] (FDA) | date=18 December 2014 | url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/204977Orig1s000TOC.cfm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201102031112/https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2014/204977Orig1s000TOC.cfm | archive-date=2 November 2020 | access-date=24 November 2024}}</ref>

extract:
Omega-3-acid ethyl esters are a mixture of ethyl eicosapentaenoate and ethyl docosahexaenoate, which are ethyl esters of the omega−3 fatty acids eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) found in fish oil. Together with dietary changes, they are used to treat high blood triglycerides which may reduce the risk of pancreatitis. They are generally less preferred than statins, and use is not recommended by NHS Scotland as the evidence does not support a decreased risk of heart disease. Omega-3-acid ethyl esters are taken by mouth.
Common side effects include burping, nausea, and an upset abdomen. Serious side effects may include liver problems and anaphylaxis. While use in pregnancy has not been well studied, some omega−3 fatty acids appear beneficial. How it works is not entirely clear.
Experts found a dose-dependent increase in the risk for atrial fibrillation in patients with cardiovascular diseases or cardiovascular risk factors who were being treated with omega-3-acid ethyl esters compared with those treated with placebo. The observed risk was at its highest at a dose of 4 g/d.[1]
Omega-3-acid ethyl ester medicines were approved for medical use in the European Union in 2000 and in the United States in 2004. Beyond the branded prescription formulation, it is also available as a generic medication and over the counter. In 2023, it was the 222nd most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 1 million prescriptions.
